screens.title: Advanced Movement Mechanics & Character Controllers
screens.subtitle: From APawn to ACharacter — enabling robust jumping, sprinting, and physics-aware movement

narration.text: In this lesson we will build a practical understanding of humanoid movement in Unreal Engine using the built-in ACharacter and its UCharacterMovementComponent. You'll learn why an ACharacter is preferred over a raw APawn for bipedal movement, how to set up common mechanics like jump and sprint, and how the PlayerController fits into possession and higher-level game logic. We'll also walk through a concrete C++ example that shows the constructor configuration, input bindings for jump and sprint, and the Move and Look implementations that rely on the CharacterMovementComponent. This is important because trying to replicate the movement behavior of ACharacter on APawn is time-consuming and error prone, especially when you consider slope handling, stepping up, gravity, and network prediction. By the end you'll understand when to convert a pawn to a character, how to set MaxWalkSpeed and JumpZVelocity correctly, and which common mistakes to avoid. As you follow the code walkthrough later, notice how ACharacter's helpers like Jump and StopJumping simplify implementation and how storing a DefaultWalkSpeed makes sprinting reliable.

keyIdea.title: Why prefer ACharacter?
keyIdea.text: ACharacter brings UCapsuleComponent and UCharacterMovementComponent that handle gravity, jumping, slopes, and networked prediction so you don't reimplement complex biped movement on APawn.

narration.text: These learning objectives guide our practice in this chapter. First, you'll be able to distinguish APawn from ACharacter and decide which base class fits a given gameplay role. That means recognizing when built-in humanoid features like a capsule collider and movement component save time versus when a lightweight pawn is preferable. Second, you'll learn to use the UCharacterMovementComponent: how its properties like MaxWalkSpeed, JumpZVelocity, AirControl, and bOrientRotationToMovement affect runtime behavior. Third, you'll implement core advanced mechanics — jumping, crouching, and sprinting — using ACharacter helpers and input bindings so you get reliable, network-friendly results. Fourth, you'll understand the PlayerController's job in possession and higher-level flows, and how it connects input to the pawn or character. Each objective pairs knowledge with a competency milestone so you can verify mastery. For example, converting a pawn to ACharacter and wiring IA_Jump and IA_Sprint to Jump and sprint handlers is a practical milestone that demonstrates these skills in context.

screens.title: APawn vs ACharacter — Choose the right base class
screens.subtitle: When to use APawn and when to use ACharacter for movement needs

narration.text: Start by understanding the fundamental distinction between APawn and ACharacter. APawn is the minimal base for anything a controller can possess. It gives you a clean slate: you can attach custom components and write movement logic tailored to vehicles, flying drones, or cameras that don't need humanoid behaviors. ACharacter extends APawn and includes a UCapsuleComponent and a UCharacterMovementComponent out of the box, which implement gravity, walking, falling, jumping, slope handling, stepping, and built-in network prediction. That makes ACharacter the pragmatic choice for humanoid player characters and NPCs that walk around on the ground. A concrete example: if you're building a drivable spaceship you typically choose APawn and add a custom movement component that handles thrust and rotation. Conversely, for a third-person player who walks and jumps, choose ACharacter to avoid reimplementing collision and movement smoothing. A common misconception is that ACharacter is always heavier and therefore always wrong; instead think about required behavior. If you need bipedal physics-aware movement, ACharacter saves significant effort and reduces the risk of subtle bugs, especially in multiplayer where prediction and replication matter. APawn vs ACharacter — Choose the right base class means use apawn for lightweight, custom movement. use acharacter when you need bipedal movement and the built-in movement component features.. In practical terms, when to use apawn and when to use acharacter for movement needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison

APawn — clean slate

APawn is minimal and ideal for vehicles, flying actors, or special movement that doesn't map to bipedal walking.

  • • Lightweight base class for custom movement
  • • No capsule or CharacterMovement by default
  • • Good for spaceships, cameras, or floating drones
Example
A drivable spaceship uses APawn with a custom thrust and rotation component rather than a CharacterMovementComponent.
Comparison

ACharacter — humanoid system

ACharacter includes a UCapsuleComponent and UCharacterMovementComponent that implement gravity, walking, jumping, slope behavior, and prediction.

  • • Built-in capsule collision
  • • CharacterMovement handles Jump, gravity, and slopes
  • • Network-aware movement prediction
Example
A third-person player who walks, turns, jumps, and crouches should use ACharacter to leverage the movement component.

screens.title: UCharacterMovementComponent — what it provides
screens.subtitle: Core responsibilities and key configurable properties

narration.text: The UCharacterMovementComponent is the central engine for humanoid movement. It handles gravity, walking, falling, jumping, slope handling, step-up logic, and network prediction for characters. Practically, it means you do not manually scale input by delta seconds in AddMovementInput, because the component processes movement and integrates it with the physics system. Important properties you will configure include MaxWalkSpeed to control ground speed, JumpZVelocity to shape jump height and arc, AirControl to allow limited steering in mid-air, RotationRate to control how fast the character rotates, and bOrientRotationToMovement which makes the character face its movement direction. A concrete configuration example used in the chapter sets JumpZVelocity to 600, AirControl to 0.2, MaxWalkSpeed to 600, MinAnalogWalkSpeed to 20, and BrakingDecelerationWalking to 2000. These values are starting points that you tune for feel. Remember to store DefaultWalkSpeed at BeginPlay if you plan to temporarily change MaxWalkSpeed during sprinting, because failing to do so is a common source of bugs. screens.subtitle: Create the character class, set up components, and configure movement defaults

narration.text: Converting a pawn to a character is a straightforward sequence: create a new C++ class that inherits from ACharacter, copy or recreate your camera and spring arm setup in the constructor, and configure GetCharacterMovement properties to match desired behavior. The chapter provides a practical header layout: declare UInputMappingContext and UInputAction properties for Move, Look, Jump, and Sprint, plus SprintSpeedMultiplier and DefaultWalkSpeed members. Also set bUseControllerRotationYaw to false so controller yaw doesn't fight movement-oriented rotation. In BeginPlay, store DefaultWalkSpeed by reading GetCharacterMovement()->MaxWalkSpeed so sprint toggles can revert reliably. This flow minimizes friction: you get collision, movement, camera, and input wiring in a repeatable pattern. screens.title: Move and Look implementations
screens.subtitle: How AddMovementInput and controller input work with CharacterMovementComponent

narration.text: Movement input in ACharacter differs from a raw pawn because the CharacterMovementComponent handles time integration. In Move you read a two-dimensional input vector and convert it into forward and right directions using the controller's yaw rotation. Call AddMovementInput with the forward and right vectors and pass the input scale directly — do not multiply by delta seconds because the movement component handles that. For Look, acquire the two-axis look input and call AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput to forward values into the controller. This separation keeps camera control independent from movement velocity and rotation behavior. A concrete example demonstrates that AddMovementInput(ForwardDirection, MovementVector. Y) and AddMovementInput(RightDirection, MovementVector. X) are the correct calls. A common mistake is multiplying these vectors by delta seconds out of habit, which will produce extremely slow movement. Another subtle issue is ensuring Controller is non-null before applying rotation; check Controller!= nullptr before adding controller inputs. After implementing, test both keyboard and gamepad mapping for consistent feel. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Move & Look

Move and Look implementations

Use controller yaw to build forward/right vectors and pass raw input to AddMovementInput; use controller input functions for look.

Move example
void AMyPlayerCharacter::Move(const FInputActionValue& Value)
{
  FVector2D MovementVector = Value.Get();
  if (Controller != nullptr)
  {
    const FRotator Rotation = Controller->GetControlRotation();
    const FRotator YawRotation(0, Rotation.Yaw, 0);
    const FVector ForwardDirection = FRotationMatrix(YawRotation).GetUnitAxis(EAxis::X);
    const FVector RightDirection = FRotationMatrix(YawRotation).GetUnitAxis(EAxis::Y);
    AddMovementInput(ForwardDirection, MovementVector.Y);
    AddMovementInput(RightDirection, MovementVector.X);
  }
}
Look example
Call AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput with look axis values and ensure Controller is valid first.
Key Takeaway

Do not multiply input by delta seconds for AddMovementInput when using CharacterMovementComponent; it handles integration.

screens.title: Jumping: Jump() and StopJumping()
screens.subtitle: How ACharacter's built-in jump functions simplify implementation

narration.text: Jump behavior is already integrated into ACharacter through Jump and StopJumping. When your input mapping produces Started and Completed events, call Jump on start and StopJumping on complete. Jump uses the configured JumpZVelocity in the CharacterMovementComponent to generate a vertical impulse and the movement component handles falling and landing. A concrete example: bind IA_Jump with ETriggerEvent::Started to JumpStarted that simply calls Jump, and ETriggerEvent::Completed to JumpCompleted that calls StopJumping. This approach is safer than applying manual vertical impulses because the movement component coordinates animation, collision, and prediction for networked play. A common misconception is that StopJumping is optional; for variable-height jumps or to prevent continuous jumping, properly handling Completed events is required. Also tune JumpZVelocity and AirControl to balance jump height and mid-air steering. After wiring, test the jump arc in-editor and adjust values until the feel matches designers' intent. Jump implementation

Bind the jump input to call Jump on start and StopJumping on completion so CharacterMovement manages motion.

Binding pattern
Bind JumpAction Started -> JumpStarted -> Jump(); Completed -> JumpCompleted -> StopJumping().
Tuning
Adjust JumpZVelocity and AirControl for desired arc and mid-air control. Test on slopes and during networked play if applicable.
Common Mistake
Calling Jump without StopJumping on completion can lead to inconsistent or extended jump behavior, especially with variable-height jumps.

screens.title: Sprinting: toggling MaxWalkSpeed safely
screens.subtitle: Store DefaultWalkSpeed and scale MaxWalkSpeed during sprint

narration.text: Sprinting is a pattern of temporarily increasing MaxWalkSpeed and then restoring it. The key step is storing DefaultWalkSpeed at BeginPlay by reading GetCharacterMovement()->MaxWalkSpeed. When the sprint input starts, set GetCharacterMovement()->MaxWalkSpeed to DefaultWalkSpeed times SprintSpeedMultiplier. When the sprint input completes, set MaxWalkSpeed back to DefaultWalkSpeed. This avoids hard-coding a value you may later change in the editor and prevents drift if sprinting toggles repeatedly. The chapter shows SprintStarted and SprintCompleted functions that perform these changes. A common bug is not initializing DefaultWalkSpeed before first sprint — if you modify MaxWalkSpeed elsewhere or in Blueprints, BeginPlay ensures you capture the runtime default. Also, avoid stacking multipliers without resetting: always reset to the stored default rather than dividing or subtracting. After wiring sprint, test holding and releasing the sprint key to ensure speed returns to the original walking speed consistently. Sprint implementation

Use a stored default speed and multiply it for sprint, then restore to avoid cumulative changes.

BeginPlay store

Sprint handlers

screens.title: Rotation and orientation — avoiding conflicts
screens.subtitle: bUseControllerRotationYaw vs bOrientRotationToMovement and typical setup

narration.text: Character rotation is often a source of unexpected behavior. Two flags interact: bUseControllerRotationYaw and bOrientRotationToMovement. If bUseControllerRotationYaw is true, the controller's yaw directly drives the actor rotation. If bOrientRotationToMovement is true on the CharacterMovementComponent, the actor is rotated to face the direction of movement. If both are true simultaneously you create a conflict: the character will try to face both the controller yaw and the movement direction and this manifests as jittery or incorrect rotation. The recommended setup for third-person movement is to set bUseControllerRotationYaw to false on the character and enable bOrientRotationToMovement so the mesh rotates toward the movement vector while the camera can still use pawn control rotation through the spring arm. A short example from the chapter sets bUseControllerRotationYaw = false in the constructor and GetCharacterMovement()->bOrientRotationToMovement = true. Always test rotation during strafing, camera rotation, and moving while looking around to validate the feel. Rotation and orientation — avoiding conflicts means disable controller yaw on the character and enable orientation to movement for movement-driven rotation; avoid enabling both simultaneously.. In practical terms, busecontrollerrotationyaw vs borientrotationtomovement and typical setup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Rotation rule

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Rotation & Orientation

Avoid rotation conflicts

Either let the controller directly rotate the pawn or let the movement component orient the mesh — don't do both.

• If you want character to face movement direction, set bUseControllerRotationYaw = false and bOrientRotationToMovement = true.
• If you want controller-driven facing, set bUseControllerRotationYaw = true and disable bOrientRotationToMovement.
• Test combinations during gameplay; jitter indicates conflicting rotation inputs.
Quick Fix
Set bUseControllerRotationYaw = false in constructor and GetCharacterMovement()->bOrientRotationToMovement = true to produce expected movement-aligned facing.
Common Bug
Enabling both flags causes jerky rotation because two systems fight to set actor yaw.

screens.title: PlayerController and Possession
screens.subtitle: How possession links input to pawn/character and where to place higher-level logic

narration.text: APlayerController is the player's 'brain'. When a player joins, the engine creates a PlayerController and that controller possesses an APawn or ACharacter. Possession links input handling to the pawn, routing player actions through SetupPlayerInputComponent and the pawn's bindings. PlayerController is also the place for higher-level game logic that doesn't belong in a single pawn — HUD management, pausing, menu interaction, or matchmaking. Keep movement-specific code in the character and UI or persistent session logic in the controller. A practical tip: ensure your GameMode assigns the correct default pawn class so the PlayerController possesses the character you expect at BeginPlay. In multiplayer, PlayerController instances exist on the client and server, while possession and replication rules determine how input affects movement and how CharacterMovementComponent performs prediction. Test possession scenarios by manually possessing a pawn in editor to validate that inputs are routed and HUD elements respond correctly. PlayerController and Possession means use playercontroller for player-specific and hud logic; keep movement and per-character behavior inside the pawn or character class.. narration.text: Let's summarize the essential terms you should remember. First: ACharacter — a specialized APawn for humanoid movement that provides capsule collision and a CharacterMovementComponent. Second: UCharacterMovementComponent — the movement system for characters, responsible for gravity, walking, jumping, slope handling, and network prediction. Third: UCapsuleComponent — the typical collision primitive used as a character's root so collision and step-up behavior are consistent. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Mechanics & Pitfalls
Sprint safety
Capture DefaultWalkSpeed in BeginPlay and restore it when sprint ends to avoid speed drift.
Input scaling
Do not multiply AddMovementInput by delta seconds when using CharacterMovementComponent; it integrates motion for you.
Rotation conflict
Avoid enabling both bUseControllerRotationYaw and bOrientRotationToMovement to prevent jerky rotation.
Final Tip
Test movement features early in the editor and in multiplayer when applicable to catch prediction and replication issues.
